statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands, production lots and reading rules. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone. Because the forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS to find could enter this positive group, so how often strips miss samples with very little fentanyl was not measured (Green et al., 2020). Second-hand figures, relayed without their conditions, mostly point the same way: in British Columbia drug-checking data, 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples were missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024); and another paper relays 87.5 in 100 from a validation study (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards prepared in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration, counting a faint test band as positive (the pictured strips at 25 and 50 ng/mL show a faint band, which the makers' rule, any visible band means negative, reads as negative; Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on all four brands in the main table, two of them with only a barely visible test band that the makers' rule reads as negative, and, in a descending series pictured for two brands, down to 50 and 25 ng/mL by the authors' rule (100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule), with no replicates reported and one brand graded differently at 100 ng/mL in the table and the figure (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL, from a heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024): a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips showed fentanyl in almost all drug samples that contained it: 104 of 106 police-seized samples in one study. All those samples had enough fentanyl for the laboratory's own machine to find it; samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way. Strips can pick up very small amounts, but the smallest amount they found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches of strips, and also depended on whether a faint line was counted. Trained staff did these tests, mostly with one brand; how well strips work when people test at home was not measured.

magnitude: Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation); reference GC/MS limits 3.1 and 100 µg/mL. Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye, counting a faint band (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only, and in a pictured series down to 50 ng/mL (Rapid Response) and 25 ng/mL (One Step) by the authors' rule, 100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL, heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024); 87.5% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al., 2022).

risk_of_bias.note: Every laboratory study is at high risk of bias by QUADAS-2 (study cards): Green et al. selected samples on known GC/MS status (106 with and 104 without fentanyl) and used a reference less sensitive than the strip, so samples with little fentanyl could not enter the positive group; Bergh et al. graded bands after seeing them, with readers not described as blind; Halifax et al. tested old and new lots in different rounds; Lockwood et al.'s limit counts a faint band that its own stated reading rule calls negative. These problems bear on specificity, on borderline readings and on sensitivity for samples with little fentanyl; counted once.

inconsistency.note: Sensitivity on real samples comes from one study (Green et al.) and agrees with second-hand drug-checking data (4 of 173 missed); a lower second-hand figure (87.5 in 100) comes without its conditions and is not counted. Detection limits span 25-fold (20 to 500 ng/mL); the claim states the range, and part of it follows lot, brand and reading rule (Halifax et al.; Bergh et al.; Lockwood et al.), so it is not rated down again.

indirectness.note: Trained laboratory staff, pure fentanyl in water or ethanol or seized samples tested as powders, mostly one brand; people ask how strips work on their own drugs at home.

imprecision.note: 104 of 106 (95% CI 93.4–99.5%); detection limits from replicated strips in most studies (triplicates, Green et al. and Sisco et al., 2024b; five strips per level, Lockwood et al.; duplicates on five lots, Halifax et al.); no replicates are reported in Bergh et al.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence that compares the strip with a reference method starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of fentanyl in seized samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS and in pure solutions, not home use and not effects on behaviour or overdose, which are separate questions. Status replicated: independent teams in five laboratories (Green et al.; Lockwood et al.; Bergh et al.; Halifax et al.; Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024) detected fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations; only Green et al. measured sensitivity on seized samples. Overlap: the review's sensitivity range comes from a study sharing authors with Green et al. and from the drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al., so it is not counted separately, and the figure relayed by Klaire et al. is second-hand and not counted. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (card sc_sisco_2024b) and adds one detection limit, from its heat sub-study.

statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips on dissolved samples that contained no fentanyl, compared with laboratory analysis or known content, strips sometimes read positive, mostly with strong solutions of a few other drugs. Among 104 police-seized samples without fentanyl by earlier GC/MS, one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 6 (1 of 52 in one laboratory, 5 of 52 in the other; specificity 94.2%, editors' Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, so about 6 in 100 read falsely positive); the five described held only buprenorphine, heroin (two), methamphetamine or noscapine, and because the GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip, some may have held traces of fentanyl or of a fentanyl analogue that the GC/MS methods did not find (Green et al., 2020). In solutions made in the laboratory, strong concentrations of four substances turned the strip positive with no fentanyl present: methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine and lidocaine. With one strip per concentration, solutions of one seized methamphetamine sample, one seized MDMA sample and retail diphenhydramine tablets and capsules read positive by eye above about 2 mg/mL of material and, by image analysis, from 1 to 2.5 mg/mL, while seized cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products read negative up to 20 mg/mL (Lockwood et al., 2021). With pure standards and duplicate strips on five lots, the thresholds for lots obtained in 2017 and in 2021 were 5 and 10 mg/mL for d-methamphetamine, 50 and 2.5–5 mg/mL for MDMA and 100 and 2.5 mg/mL for lidocaine; diphenhydramine read positive from 0.5–1 mg/mL on the 2021 lots but, unexpectedly, negative or invalid at 50 mg/mL and negative on two of three lots at 100 mg/mL, while the 2017 lots, positive at 100 mg/mL, were not tested below 50 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine (25 mg/mL), cocaine and ketamine (25 mg/mL) and levamisole (up to 100 mg/mL) did not react (Halifax et al., 2024). Twelve other drugs, among them amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine, gave no false positive on four brands at 100 or 1000 ng/mL, far below the concentrations that gave false positives elsewhere, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) at 10 mg/mL or more did so on one brand only (Bergh et al., 2021). Within the same strips, the lowest concentration that gave a false positive was 2,500 times (Halifax et al., lots obtained in 2021: 0.5 mg/mL against a fentanyl limit of 200 ng/mL) to about 40,000 times (Lockwood et al.: 1 mg/mL of material against 25 ng/mL) the lowest fentanyl concentration detected (editors' calculation). Second-hand, from validation studies and drug-checking data not read here and relayed without their conditions, specificity was about 89 in 100 (Kutscher et al., 2024) and 95 in 100 (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). Outside the laboratory, people using take-home strips reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples and 16 of 93 cocaine samples, against 5 of 97 and 1 of 92 other samples tested on site by staff, which the authors attribute mostly to false positives from how samples were prepared (Klaire et al., 2022; different samples, nothing confirmed, not tested). A scoping review lists cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam and buprenorphine-naloxone among causes of false positives, citing Lockwood et al., who found these four negative up to 20 mg/mL, and a validation study not read here (Kutscher et al., 2024). How often false positives happen when people test their own drugs, and whether a stimulant mixed with fentanyl changes the reading, were not measured; ways of preparing samples that authors proposed to avoid false positives were not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Yes, sometimes. In laboratory tests, strong solutions of methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine (an allergy and sleep medicine) or lidocaine (a numbing medicine used as a cutting agent) made fentanyl strips read positive with no fentanyl present. It took thousands of times more of these drugs than the smallest amount of fentanyl the same strips could find. In one study of seized drugs, about 6 in 100 samples without fentanyl read positive. How often this happens when people test their own drugs is not known.

exposure: Urine fentanyl immunoassay test strips used off-label on dissolved drug (BTNX Rapid Response in three studies; four brands in one), read by laboratory staff by eye or by image analysis
comparator: Earlier GC/MS analysis showing no fentanyl, or the known content of prepared solutions
outcome: False-positive fentanyl readings, and the concentrations of other substances at which they occurred
magnitude: Green et al.: specificity 98.1% (51/52) and 90.4% (47/52); 6/104 false positives (5.8%; specificity 94.2%, Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, editors' calculation). Lockwood et al. (weighed material, not pure drug; one strip per concentration): by eye above about 2 mg/mL; by image analysis diphenhydramine capsules 1, methamphetamine 1.5, MDMA 2, diphenhydramine tablets 2.5 mg/mL (about 0.10 and 0.25 mg/mL of diphenhydramine HCl, editors' calculation on the card); negative up to 20 mg/mL: cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products. Halifax et al. (pure standards; 2017 lots against 2021 lots): d-methamphetamine 5 against 10; MDMA 50 against 2.5–5; lidocaine 100 against 2.5 mg/mL; diphenhydramine 0.5–1 mg/mL on the 2021 lots, negative or invalid at 50 mg/mL and negative at 100 mg/mL on two of three lots, the 2017 lots positive at 100 mg/mL and not tested below 50 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine negative at 25 mg/mL; cocaine and ketamine negative at 25 mg/mL (2017 lots); levamisole none to 100 mg/mL (2021 lots). Bergh et al.: 12 non-fentanyl drugs negative at 100 and 1000 ng/mL on four brands; ascorbic acid 10 mg/mL or more positive on One Step only. Lowest false-positive concentration against the same strips' fentanyl limit (editors' calculation): 2,500 times (Halifax et al., 2021 lots) and about 40,000 times (Lockwood et al.). Second-hand specificity: 89.2–89.4% (via Kutscher et al.); 95.2% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al.). Klaire et al. (different samples, unconfirmed): crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed; 27.5% by the counts) take-home against 5/97 (5.2%) on site; cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%).

statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips, mostly on single fentanyl analogues dissolved in water and compared with the known content of each solution, the strips reacted to most analogues tested, many of them only at concentrations well above those at which they detect fentanyl, and to a few not at all. With four brands and 28 analogues graded by the authors (no test band or a barely visible one counted as positive; no replicates reported), 21, 19, 15 and 22 analogues read positive at 1000 ng/mL and 24, 24, 21 and 24 at up to 10 000 ng/mL, but only 5, 5, 12 and 9 of the 23 measured at 100 ng/mL; under the makers' rule, which counts any visible test band as negative, fewer were positive (editors' recount on the study card: 20, 20, 19 and 21 of 28 at the highest concentrations). No brand detected alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl or norcarfentanil; carfentanil read positive on no brand at 1000 ng/mL (a faint, weak or ambiguous test band on three brands, a solid band on the fourth), positive at 4000 ng/mL on three brands, and never on the fourth (Bergh et al., 2021). Five lots of one brand all detected 11 of the 13 analogues tested, carfentanil among them, with limits that differed between lots: carfentanil from 500 ng/mL on two lots obtained in 2017 but only from 10 000 ng/mL on two of three lots obtained in 2021; sufentanil was detected only by the 2017 lots, and only from 10 000 ng/mL; no lot detected alfentanil or the non-fentanyl opioid U-47700 at any concentration tested, up to 50 000 ng/mL (Halifax et al., 2024; per-lot values from the paper's figure). In four police-seized samples containing acetyl fentanyl or furanyl fentanyl, one brand read positive in all four, a set of four samples only (Green et al., 2020). Four analogues too dilute to show alone (10 ng/mL each) read positive when mixed, on the one brand tested (Bergh et al.). A scoping review relays, without concentrations or brands, that carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl test negative (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand); in the two laboratory studies read here, carfentanil read negative at lower concentrations and positive at higher ones. The analogue panels were not chosen by how often each compound occurs in drug markets, and results came from pure compounds rather than mixtures. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In laboratory tests, fentanyl strips reacted to most drugs related to fentanyl, but some only in larger amounts than fentanyl itself, and a few never. Carfentanil showed up only in large amounts, never on one of four brands, and on two of three newer batches of another brand only in very large amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by laboratory staff, with no repeat tests reported in the largest study.

statement: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips of different brands, production lots and ages did not perform the same, compared with the known content of prepared solutions. Lots: in one laboratory, two lots of one brand (BTNX Rapid Response, urine cut-off 20 ng/mL) obtained in 2017 detected fentanyl in water down to 20 ng/mL, while three lots obtained in 2021 detected it only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher, and in urine, the strips' intended use, down to 50–100 ng/mL; the 2021 lots also gave false positives with lidocaine and MDMA at concentrations 10 to 40 times lower than the 2017 lots, with d-methamphetamine at a twofold higher one (editors' calculation), and with diphenhydramine from 0.5–1 mg/mL, a range in which the 2017 lots were not tested. The two sets were tested in separate rounds (2017 and 2022), with storage and expiry not reported, so lot, storage and testing round cannot be separated (Halifax et al., 2024). Brands: on the same solutions, four brands detected 5 to 12 of the 23 analogues measured at 100 ng/mL (editors' count); one brand (One Step), which detected the most of them at 100 ng/mL, read negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at every concentration, which the other three detected at higher concentrations, and it alone gave false positives with ascorbic acid at 10 mg/mL or more (Bergh et al., 2021). Heat and age: strips with a listed cut-off of 200 ng/mL detected 500 ng/mL whether or not they had been kept unopened at 55 °C for two weeks; strips with a listed cut-off of 20 ng/mL, more than four years past expiry and kept in laboratory conditions, detected 250 ng/mL, but no in-date strips of that kind were tested (the in-date strips tested, listed at 200 ng/mL, were apparently a different product or version), so the effect of age cannot be separated from the product (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024; apparently one lot each, triplicates). In another laboratory, diphenhydramine solutions tested at 4 °C read positive on every strip at all three concentrations tried, while at 25 and 40 °C the readings followed concentration; no drug-free (water) blank or fentanyl solution was reported at 4 °C (Lockwood et al., 2021). How strips perform after storage as people keep them, after longer heat, or across many lots and brands was not measured. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: No. In laboratory tests, batches of one brand bought in 2021 needed ten times more fentanyl to show it than batches bought in 2017, and four brands differed in which related drugs they picked up. Two weeks of heat did not change one kind of strip. Strips more than four years out of date still worked but needed more fentanyl than their label said; no new strips of the same kind were tested to compare. Why batches differed could not be worked out from these studies.
population: Fentanyl, fentanyl analogues and other substances in water or drug-free urine, tested in laboratories
exposure: Fentanyl test strips of different brands (four), production lots (five lots of one brand, obtained in 2017 or 2021) and ages or storage (in date, kept unopened at 55 °C for two weeks, or more than four years past expiry); one test temperature of 4 °C
comparator: Known content of each solution, and the brands, lots and ages compared with each other
outcome: Lowest fentanyl concentration detected, analogue detection and false-positive thresholds
magnitude: Halifax et al.: fentanyl in water 20 ng/mL (2017 lots) against 200 ng/mL (2021 lots); in urine 50 and 100 ng/mL (2021 lots); false-positive thresholds 2017 against 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 5 against 10, MDMA 50 against 2.5–5, lidocaine 100 against 2.5 mg/mL; diphenhydramine 0.5–1 mg/mL on the 2021 lots, not comparable with the 2017 lots, which were tested only at 50 mg/mL and above (positive at 100). Bergh et al.: analogues at 100 ng/mL 5, 5, 12 and 9 of 23 measured by brand (editors' count); One Step negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at all concentrations; ascorbic acid false positives on One Step only. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024): fentanyl strips 0.5 µg/mL heated or not (listed 0.2 µg/mL); expired fentanyl strips of another kind 0.25 µg/mL (listed 0.02 µg/mL); expired methamphetamine strips 5 against 1 µg/mL; expired cocaine strips unchanged at 2.5 µg/mL. Lockwood et al.: at 4 °C all diphenhydramine strips positive at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL.

statement: In laboratory tests of the first commercial nitazene test strip (BTNX Rapid Response; maker's cut-off 2000 ng/mL isotonitazene) on pure nitazene standards in water and on nearly pure powders from drug-market monitoring, compared with known content, the strips detected most nitazenes tested but missed six of the seven desnitazenes tested and three other analogues. Read from photographs by two blinded raters and by image analysis, isotonitazene read positive in all six replicates from 3000 ng/mL with one lot and 2000 ng/mL with another, obtained about four months apart. With one lot and one strip per concentration, 24 of 33 nitazene analogues read positive at 9000 ng/mL or less; nine did not at 9000 ng/mL: six desnitazenes, which lack the 5-nitro group (among them metodesnitazene and etodesnitazene), 5-aminoisotonitazene and two analogues with a longer link between the rings; the seventh desnitazene tested, 5-methyl etodesnitazene, was detected. Six powders obtained in Belgian drug-market monitoring, each estimated as more than 90% one nitazene, all read positive at about 1 and 0.1 mg/mL (6 of 6; editors' Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%) (De Vrieze et al., 2024). In a second laboratory, the strips detected metonitazene from 1 µg/mL and N-piperidinyl etonitazene and protonitazene from 5 µg/mL (ten strips per level), and reacted to none of 76 other drugs, cutting agents and other compounds at two concentrations (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). No study read tested nitazene-free street samples or mixtures in which a nitazene is a small part of heroin, other opioids or stimulants, so how often the strips miss nitazenes or give false positives in real samples is unknown; preliminary street-sample figures cited from the maker's material (12 samples) are unpublished. The first study's authors write that a negative result does not mean a sample is free of nitazenes or safe, and that a positive one does not show which nitazene is present or how much. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, read positive in nearly all residue samples with at least the strip's listed amount of xylazine, read positive on every strip in pure solutions only from 2.5 times that amount, and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%; the one miss had 2 µg/mL) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not at that concentration, the only one tested, so at that level these strips would not show them; higher concentrations, as from dissolved powders, were not tested (Sisco, Nestadt, et al., 2024). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.

With smaller amounts they often missed it, and in pure water every strip read positive only at 2.5 times that amount. At the one amount tested, they did not react to medetomidine, a similar animal sedative. One batch of strips was tested, on residues wiped from used equipment rather than on powders.

statement: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read at the sites, after infrared spectroscopy of the same sample and with one combined result recorded, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples from five of the sites, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 times or more the concentrations at which it detected the others (editors' calculation) (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). A report relayed second-hand by Laing et al. concluded that newer benzodiazepines appear to be detected by similar strips, etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than other NPS benzodiazepines, still within the range useful for drug checking (Shapiro et al., 2020), so the sources disagree on whether these strips react to etizolam at all; differences in lots or test conditions may explain it, but this was not shown. Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Often not. At one drug-checking service, benzodiazepine strips missed 9 of 24 samples that held a newer benzodiazepine, and half of the samples with etizolam alone. They also read positive in about 16 in 100 samples with none. In a laboratory, the same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam, though an earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up in larger amounts. Few samples were checked by a laboratory, and many were chosen after suspected overdoses.
population: Drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey, Canada (2018 to 2020), of which 153 had confirmatory laboratory results; benzodiazepines in water in a second laboratory
exposure: BTNX benzodiazepine urine test strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL) used on dissolved drug at the sites after FTIR of the same sample, with one combined result recorded; the same maker's strip in pure solutions
comparator: Confirmatory laboratory testing (GC–MS, LC-MS or qNMR) for NPS benzodiazepines; known content of prepared solutions
outcome: Detection of NPS benzodiazepines (sensitivity), false positives, and detection of individual benzodiazepines in water
magnitude: Laing et al. (153 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results; 6 with only typical benzodiazepines removed): strips 15/24 NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%; Wilson 42.7–78.8%, editors' calculation), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20/129 negatives positive (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); 87.5% (n = 8) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam; 50.0% (n = 16; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone; FTIR 2/24 (false-negative rate 91.7%), false-positive rate 3.9%; either method 17/24 detected, 23 false positives. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024): limits 0.1 µg/mL (diazepam, alprazolam) and 0.25 µg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); etizolam negative from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 to 100 times or more those limits (editors' calculation). Second-hand (Shapiro et al., 2020, via Laing et al.): similar strips appear to detect etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than flualprazolam and flubromazolam.

FTIR: of 7 positives, 5 had no NPS benzodiazepine (false-positive rate 3.9%); 22 of 146 FTIR negatives contained one (false-negative rate 91.7%); FTIR identified 2 etizolam samples that were negative on strips. Editors' calculation: 129 confirmed negatives (20 + 109 in Table 3); Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8% for 15/24 and 10.3–22.7% for 20/129; 8 of 16 etizolam-only samples (28.0–72.0%).

evidence.extracted: Point-of-care testing was done in two steps: 2–3 mg of the sample analysed by FTIR, then dissolved in water and tested with strips, with one combined result recorded; who read the strips and the water volume are not stated. Confirmatory samples came from five of the eight sites (three in Vancouver, two in Surrey). Second-hand: a report on similar strips (Shapiro et al., 2020) concluded that flualprazolam and flubromazolam appear to be detected at concentrations similar to alprazolam, and etizolam at a higher minimum concentration that was still within the range useful for drug checking; the authors cite it as recent evidence of cross-reactivity supporting point-of-care use. The report was not read.

risk_of_bias.note: Laing et al. compares strips with confirmatory tests inside programme data (filed cross-sectional with JBI-prevalence, high, on the card) and is treated as accuracy evidence with high risk of bias: only 159 of 1368 point-of-care-tested samples were verified, chosen for convenience and partly because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose; the strip was read after FTIR of the same sample with one combined result recorded; the targeted two-laboratory reference disagreed on 2 of 7 duplicate samples; strip lots were not reported. The biases can run in either direction; very serious, two levels.

inconsistency.note: Both primary studies find etizolam poorly detected; the difference in degree (half of etizolam-only samples positive in programme data, never in pure solution) may reflect other reacting compounds, untargeted benzodiazepines, lots or conditions, and is reported in the claim; the second-hand report that similar strips detected etizolam at higher concentrations is not counted, so not rated down.

indirectness.note: Strips read at harm-reduction sites in one urban area (2018 to 2020) and pure solutions in a laboratory; one brand, made for urine.

imprecision.note: 24 confirmed positives (interval 43 to 79 in 100) and 16 etizolam-only samples.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; Laing et al.'s agreement figures are accuracy evidence with high risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), so two levels for risk of bias and one each for indirectness and imprecision take it to the floor of very low. Rated as worded. Status replicated: independent teams (British Columbia; NIST) both found etizolam poorly detected; Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round; the Shapiro et al. report is second-hand and not counted.

statement: In one laboratory study of a three-reagent colour kit for ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents; two identical DanceSafe kits bought online, without lot numbers), compared with GC-MS or the known identity of the drugs, readings by experienced analysts matched whether MDMA was present, readings by two testers new to the kit did not, and a positive reading never showed a second drug. Three experienced analysts using the kit's instructions and colour charts read all 35 seized samples that contained MDMA as positive and the four without MDMA as negative, except that one analyst read one of the four, which held no identifiable drug, as weakly positive (editors' Wilson 95% CI 90.1–100% for 35 of 35, 51.0–100% for 4 of 4); the seven MDMA samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA read like the rest. Two testers trained in pharmacology but new to the kit, given eight samples of known drugs and only the kit's leaflet, diverged: one read both MDMA samples as negative, the other read codeine, dihydrocodeine, dextromethorphan and morphine as MDMA or MDMA-like; together 2 of 4 MDMA readings were positive and 7 of 12 non-MDMA readings negative, and with the Marquis reagent alone 10 of the 12 non-MDMA readings were positive (Murray et al., 2003). A laboratory comparison from an unpublished thesis, known only from a narrative review (156 amnesty-bin samples, Marquis read by laboratory staff before GC-MS), found the MDMA colour (purple, blue or black) in all 53 samples with MDMA-like substances and in no others, but 14 other samples gave a purple/violet reading that staff filed as the opiate colour, and 43 presumptive colour readings in all had no matching drug (editors' sum); its table holds 187 entries for 156 samples (Winstock et al., 2001). Two narrative reviews add, second-hand, that colour tests are presumptive, that other substances react too (the Marquis reagent also with aspirin and sugar) and that more than one drug or tablet dyes can change the result (Philp & Fu, 2018; Winstock et al., 2001); one adds that MDMA, MDEA and MDA give similar colours and that, read by eye, the tests show nothing about a pill's strength (Winstock et al., 2001). No sample contained PMA, MDA or methamphetamine, and the kit and drug market were those of the early 2000s. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one laboratory study from 2003, experts reading a three-reagent colour kit got MDMA right in all 35 samples that had it, and nearly always right in the 4 without it. But the colour looked the same when another drug was mixed in, and two people new to the kit made many mistakes, calling several other drugs MDMA. Read by eye, colour tests do not show how much MDMA is in a pill.
population: 39 police and laboratory evidence samples sold as MDMA and eight samples of known drugs (one US laboratory, early 2000s); 156 amnesty-bin samples from a London dance venue (second-hand)
exposure: A three-reagent colour test kit for ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke, Simon's), read by experienced analysts or by two testers new to the kit; the Marquis reagent in the second-hand comparison
comparator: GC-MS of the same samples, or the known identity of the drugs supplied
outcome: Agreement of colour readings with laboratory results on whether MDMA or an MDMA-like substance was present, and what the readings did not show
magnitude: Murray et al. Part I (experienced analysts, three reagents): 35/35 MDMA samples positive (Wilson 90.1–100%, editors' calculation); 4/4 non-MDMA negative for two analysts (51.0–100%), 3/4 for the third (one weak positive); 7 samples with a second drug read like MDMA alone. Part II (two novices, 8 known drugs, three reagents): sensitivity 2/4 (50%), specificity 7/12 (58%), positive and negative predictive values 2/7 and 7/9 (printed 28% and 77%); Novice A 0/2 MDMA detected and 5/6 others negative, Novice B 2/2 and 2/6; Marquis alone 10 false positives in 12 non-MDMA readings and 2 false negatives. Winstock et al. (second-hand, Murphy 1999): purple/blue/black 53/53 MDMA-like and 0 others; orange/brown 47 amphetamine samples and 21 without; yellow/green 8 and purple/violet 14 with no matching GC-MS class (43 in all, editors' sum); 187 cell entries for n = 156.

evidence.locator: Table 2 and footnote (p. 1240); Results › Part I, 1st paragraph (p. 1241)
evidence.extracted: Three analysts, experienced chemists familiar with reagent use, tested with Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents: each recorded 35 positives; GC-MS found MDMA in all 35, seven of them also with caffeine, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA. Of the four samples without MDMA (alprazolam; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with guaifenesin; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with caffeine; no identifiable drug), Analysts 2 and 3 recorded four negatives and Analyst 1 three negatives and one weak positive (the sample with no identifiable drug). The analysts disagreed on exact colours but generally agreed on whether MDMA was present; Marquis alone gave similar results, not shown. Editors' calculation: Wilson 95% CI 90.1–100% for 35/35 and 51.0–100% for 4/4.

evidence.locator: Results › Part II, 1st paragraph; Table 3 and footnotes
evidence.extracted: Two testers, professionals in pharmacology and toxicology inexperienced with the kits, given the kit, its labelling and eight blinded samples (codeine, dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine, ketamine, MDMA twice, morphine, d-norpropoxyphene): sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values 50%, 58%, 28% and 77% for both testers together with all three reagents. Novice A called only morphine positive (for an MDMA-like substance) and both MDMA samples negative; Novice B called all but ketamine and d-norpropoxyphene positive for MDMA or an MDMA-like substance. With Marquis alone each tester had five false positives, and Novice A two false negatives. One tester was slightly injured by a drop of reagent.

The narrative reviews (Winstock et al.; Philp & Fu) qualify the claim and are labelled second-hand.

statement: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites, used at home on 55 in 100 result sheets, in alleys and streets on 22 and at supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites on 29, more than one setting possible; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6% as printed) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. By design no sample was tested both ways, and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from three US syringe services programme studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study, as its complete reference list confirms, and holds only for crystal methamphetamine); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study, with design and testers not stated, in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: When people tested their own drugs with strips they took home (used at home a little over half the time), the share of opioid samples showing fentanyl was about the same as when staff tested other samples on site (90 against 89 in 100). statement: In the studies read, a test that showed one drug did not show what else was in the sample or, read by eye, how much drug it held, and no study measured whether a negative result means a sample is less risky. A colour kit read by experienced analysts gave the same positive MDMA reading for seven samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA as for samples of MDMA alone (Murray et al., 2003). In drug-checking samples in the Vancouver area, 24 of 159 contained a newer benzodiazepine that the person had not expected (most expected fentanyl), 17 of them also held fentanyl, and infrared spectroscopy alone, which can identify several components, listed fentanyl in only 3 of those 17 and a benzodiazepine in 2 of the 24 (editors' count from the paper's table; Laing et al., 2021). Each strip type reacts to one drug or family and missed related drugs in laboratory tests: xylazine strips did not react to medetomidine or several other sedatives at the concentration tested (Sisco, Nestadt, et al., 2024), and nitazene, fentanyl and benzodiazepine strips missed some nitazenes, fentanyl analogues and etizolam (see the answers on each strip). Fentanyl strips are built to show presence only, not concentration, purity or which analogue (Green et al., 2020); in pure solutions the test band became fainter as the fentanyl concentration rose, but the makers' rule reads only whether a band is there (Bergh et al., 2021), no study read tested whether a line's strength shows how much drug a sample holds, and a scoping review lists that belief among mistaken ones (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand). The authors of the nitazene study state that a negative result does not mean a sample is safe and that a positive one gives no amount (De Vrieze et al., 2024); the xylazine study's authors, that sedatives the strips miss could give a false sense of safety (Sisco, Nestadt, et al., 2024); and a critique, that colour tests show neither many harmful substances nor a pill's strength (Winstock et al., 2001); these are their conclusions, not tested findings. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

statement: In people who use drugs in North America who were offered fentanyl test strips, or who attended services that hand them out (studies from 2016 to 2023), how many used them varied widely with the setting and with what was counted. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017) that gave 93 young adults ten strips each, with training and naloxone, and paid them to come back, 62 of the 81 analysed (83 returned at least two weeks later) said they had used at least one (77 in 100; 62 of all 93, or 67 in 100, editors' calculation), a median of 3 strips, and 10 had used all ten; 58 in 100 had given strips to others. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), where staff offered a check to every client, about 1 in 100 visits included one (1,411 of 134,176 visits, by an unknown number of people). At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 of the 732 clients analysed (57 in 100) said they had used strips in the past 30 days. A scoping review of 91 articles to March 2023 relays documented use from 1 to 80 in 100 (median 19), against stated willingness of 43 to 85 in 100 in five studies; but its supplementary table shows what the use figures are: in 13 of 14 study samples (2016 to 2021), the share who reported having used strips before, without saying whether strips had been offered to them, from 1 in 100 people seeking inpatient opioid withdrawal care to 81 in 100 people at a syringe services programme (the text says 80); the 14th is the Vancouver site's 1,411 of 134,176 visits, the same data as above. The Rhode Island pilot is not in that table. A British Columbia take-home programme did not report how many kits it handed out, so its rate of use is unknown. Use was self-reported or recorded by services, and was not checked. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.

A review's figures of about 1 to 80 in 100 mostly count something else: how many people in each study said they had used strips before it began, not how many used strips the study gave them. statement: In people who use drugs in North America who tested their drugs (or, in some studies, their urine) with fentanyl test strips, on their own without supervision or with staff at a supervised injection site (2016 to 2023), a result showing fentanyl was followed, by people's own account or by intentions they stated to staff, by a safer way of using in a minority to a majority of cases, most often using less, going slower or using with someone else around, and seldom by throwing the drug away; in each primary study read, fewer than half said they used, or would use, less; in the largest, most results were followed by using the same amount, and there a result not showing fentanyl was followed more often than one showing it by reports of using more; no study read observed what people then took. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017), of 31 young adults who said a strip had shown fentanyl, 45 in 100 said they then used smaller amounts, 42 went slower, 39 used with someone else around, 36 tried a small amount first (a 'tester'), 10 threw the drugs out, 10 sold them and 7 gave them away; these answers were given at least two weeks later, the results were not checked, and how many used the drugs as usual was not reported. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), staff recorded an intention to use less after 142 of 391 checks before use that showed fentanyl (36 in 100), against 7 of 122 that did not (6 in 100), and an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 (11 in 100) against 10 of 134 (7 in 100); what people then did was not recorded. In a British Columbia take-home programme (2019), asked a standard question (not about their own results) about what they did when a strip showed fentanyl, 217 of 336 answers (65 in 100) described no change, 86 (26 in 100) at least one safer change and 6 (2 in 100) a riskier one (using alone, or using more or faster). In a Baltimore pilot (2018 to 2019), women who sell or trade sex and use opioids were given five strips with training, counselling and naloxone; on average 56 days later, of 48 who answered about a result showing fentanyl (more than one answer allowed), 33 (69 in 100) reported at least one safer action, most often using a smaller amount (15, 31 in 100) or going slower when injecting (10, 21 in 100), while 30 (63 in 100) used the tested drugs, several because of withdrawal, 3 threw the drugs out, 3 sold them and none stopped using drugs; of 24 who answered about a result not showing fentanyl, 21 used their drugs as intended (Park et al., 2020). In a cohort of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in Kentucky, New York and Ohio who tested at least once over four weeks in 2023 and reported each week, for up to two tests a day, what they had done because of the result (Gelberg et al., 2025), the modelled probabilities after a result showing fentanyl, against one not showing it, were, for the amount used, the same 85 against 75 in 100, less or none 9 against 2 in 100, and more 6 against 23 in 100; and, for other actions, using with someone else 41 against 38 in 100, taking turns with someone 24 against 19 in 100, using near someone with naloxone 23 against 15 in 100, a smaller test amount first 12 against 10 in 100, and throwing the drugs away or not using them 1 to 2 in 100 after either result. The cohort's abstract calls the contrast a four-fold reduction in the amount used, but it is a proportional-odds ratio for reporting a smaller rather than a larger amount, not a measured fall in amount, and in absolute terms the gap lies more in reports of using more than in reports of using less; results and behaviour were self-reported and not checked, and the 541 analysed were those of 1,156 enrolled who completed the surveys, used drugs and tested. A scoping review relays a median of 55 in 100 (23 to 75 in 100, seven studies) reporting some safer change, but its supplementary table shows that the top value counts changes after each result showing fentanyl rather than people and that another is the British Columbia programme's 26 in 100 answers, counted once here; the review also relays people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl; the evidence is mostly intentions or self-reports (one review counts 22 of its 31 behaviour studies as measuring intentions), with no comparison of people given strips with people not given them; both reviews include the Rhode Island and Vancouver studies, and the scoping review the Baltimore pilot, outside its median. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When a strip showed fentanyl, some people said they used less, went slower, used with someone else nearby or tried a small amount first, but in each study fewer than half said they used, or would use, less. Few said they threw the drug away. In the largest study, most results were followed by using the same amount, and after a result without fentanyl people more often said they used more (23 in 100, against 6 in 100 after a result with fentanyl). All of this is what people said or planned: no study watched what they actually did, and no study compared people given strips with people not given them.
population: People who use drugs who tested their drugs (or, in some studies, urine) with fentanyl test strips in North America, unsupervised or with staff: 31 young adults with a self-reported positive result in a Rhode Island pilot (2017); checks before use at a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016–17); 336 survey answers from 218 people in a British Columbia take-home programme (2019); 48 women with a result showing fentanyl in a Baltimore pilot among women who sell or trade sex and use opioids (2018–19); 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in Kentucky, New York and Ohio who tested during four weeks (2023); studies relayed by a scoping review (to March 2023) and a systematic review (to October 2019)
exposure: A fentanyl test strip result showing fentanyl (a positive result)
comparator: A result not showing fentanyl (Vancouver checks, the Baltimore pilot and the three-state cohort); otherwise none
outcome: Self-reported actions after a positive result (at follow-up), intentions recorded by staff right after the result, answers to standard questions about what people did after a positive result, and actions attributed to the result, for up to two tests a day, in weekly recall, as modelled probabilities (three-state cohort)

statement: In people who had drugs tested at an English festival (2016) or with fentanyl test strips in North America (2016 to 2019), a result showing that a drug was not what it had been sold as, or that it contained fentanyl, compared with a result that did not, is associated with more people getting rid of drugs, but how many depended greatly on the setting: two thirds at the festival when the drug proved not as sold, about one in ten or fewer after a strip showed fentanyl. At one English festival, where chemists tested drugs on site and staff gave each result in a consultation, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not what it had been sold as (67 in 100) handed over drugs for police destruction, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched (9 in 100); the service saw these handovers, but people may have kept or thrown away other drugs elsewhere, and 111 of the 164 with a matching result said they would take their usual amount. After a strip showed fentanyl, few people said they would get rid of the drug, or had done so: at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 checks before use that showed fentanyl (11 in 100), against 10 of 134 that did not (7 in 100), a difference that may be chance (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.79 to 3.26), and in a Rhode Island pilot 10 in 100 of 31 young adults with a positive strip said they threw the drugs out. A systematic review of drug checking services to 2019 counts eight studies with disposal as an outcome and prints rates for four of them (editors' count), from 0 to 10 in 100 (observed at Canadian festivals at 4 and 7 in 100); it reports more disposal after unexpected results and counts this English festival among the eight without giving its rate, while an earlier evidence brief cited by the festival study gives 4 to 76 in 100 across evaluations. The authors of the Vancouver study suggest that the low rate there may reflect dependence, lack of money to replace drugs and no access to unadulterated drugs. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

statement: In people who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America, using fentanyl test strips compared with not using them: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of overdose. The only study read that compared the two groups followed 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio for four weeks in 2023: after allowing for state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and the drugs used each day, and also for strip use and risk-reduction behaviours reported during the four weeks, which may carry part of any difference strips make, the modelled risk of a self-reported overdose that people survived (passing out and needing to be revived) was about 2 in 100 days of drug use in both groups (0.02 a day; risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06, compatible with 30% fewer overdoses or twice as many); before that adjustment it was twice as high in the people who used strips (risk ratio 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89), who more often injected and used fentanyl; deaths could not be counted. A before-and-after pilot in Baltimore (2018 to 2019; Park et al., 2020), whose main planned outcome was overdose, gave five strips with training, counselling and naloxone to 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids: of the 68 followed up (66 in 100, on average 56 days later), 6 reported an overdose they survived (passing out) in the month before the start and 1 in the month before follow-up, a change that was not statistically significant and is not reported in the paper's abstract; there was no comparison group, the counselling addressed overdose risks, and the counts fell both in the 11 women who used no strip (2 to 0) and in the 57 who used at least one (4 to 1), which the paper reports separately without comparing them. A scoping review of 91 articles to March 2023 found only two that reported overdose outcomes, neither comparing people who tested with people who did not: at a supervised injection site most checks came after use (113 of the 120 overdoses were recorded with checks made after use, and a check may have been prompted by the overdose), so its lower odds of overdose among people who said they would use less (crude odds ratio 0.41) cannot show an effect; and after a vending machine began giving out strips with naloxone, county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%, with no control area. A systematic review of drug checking to 2019 found no other study linking testing with overdose. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the one study that compared people who used test strips with people who did not, over four weeks, overdoses that people survived were about as common in both groups once other differences were allowed for, but the result is too uncertain to rule out either fewer or more overdoses. That comparison also allowed for the safety steps people took during the study, which could hide a difference. Deaths could not be counted. In a small Baltimore study of women given strips, 6 reported an overdose in the month before and 1 in the month before the last visit, but there was no comparison group, and the women who used no strips also had fewer. No study read could show whether strips prevent overdoses or deaths.
population: People who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America: 732 clients of 14 strip-distributing organizations in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); 68 of 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids, followed up in a Baltimore pilot (2018–19); studies in a scoping review (to March 2023) and a systematic review of drug checking services (to October 2019)
exposure: Self-reported use of fentanyl test strips in the 30 days before baseline (cohort); strip checks at a supervised injection site, and a vending machine that dispensed strips (as relayed by the reviews); five strips with training, counselling and naloxone given to every woman (Baltimore pilot)
comparator: People at the same sites who reported no strip use (cohort); no comparison group in the two studies the scoping review describes or in the Baltimore pilot (the same women before and after)
outcome: Self-reported nonfatal overdose over four weeks (cohort); overdoses recorded by nurses with checks, and county overdose deaths and emergency visits (as relayed by the scoping review); self-reported nonfatal overdose in the month before the start and before follow-up (Baltimore pilot)
magnitude: Vickers-Smith 2025: mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), from a model that also included the number of times strips were used and the risk-reduction score during follow-up (Table 3, note g); unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710); the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02) but not in unadjusted ones: in the adjusted model the strip group's modelled risk was higher than the comparison group's in younger and lower in older participants, with 95% bands that overlap at every age (eFigure 5), and age was one of seven modifiers tested for this outcome and the only one reported (eMethods). Karamouzian 2018 (card): 113 of 120 overdoses recorded with checks made after use; crude OR 0.41 (0.18–0.89) for intended dose reduction pools checks made before and after use and is not an effect. Kutscher 2024 (relayed): 2 of 91 articles with overdose outcomes; after a vending machine (10,155 strips with naloxone in its first year), county overdose deaths fell about 10% while Ohio's rose about 5%, with no control group. Park 2020 (Baltimore, 68 of 103 followed up): nonfatal overdose in the past month 6 (8.8%) at baseline and 1 (1.5%) at follow-up, not significant; women who used no strip (n = 11) 2 to 0; women who used at least one strip (n = 57) 4 to 1, as printed in Table 3.

The Baltimore pilot: ROBINS-I critical (no comparison group; strips given with counselling and naloxone; 34 in 100 lost to follow-up; self-reports to study staff).

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness take one level each and imprecision two: very low. 'No detectable effect' would need an interval that excludes meaningful effects (METHODS §6.3), which this one does not, and the adjustment for behaviours during follow-up may also pull the estimate towards no difference, so the claim says the evidence is insufficient. Karamouzian et al.'s odds ratio of 0.41 is reported only to say why it cannot be read as an effect (card sc_karamouzian_2018, reporting issues); Karamouzian et al. is inside both reviews (the scoping review's reference 69, by its Appendix 1; card sc_kutscher_2024) and is counted once. Status single study: only one study compared people who used strips with people who did not. The Baltimore pilot (Park et al., 2020; card sc_park_2020) adds before-and-after counts (6 to 1 women) that cannot show an effect: no comparison group, strips given with counselling and naloxone, and a fall in women who used no strip as well; it reports the two groups separately without comparing them, so the status stays single study. Its overdose result, the study's main planned outcome, is not in its abstract, and the scoping review, which includes the pilot (its reference 80) among behaviour studies, did not count it among its two articles with overdose outcomes. Gelberg et al. (2025) analysed the same Stay Safe cohort as Vickers-Smith et al. for strip results and reports no overdose outcome, so it adds no comparison and is not cited here.

statement: In people who inject drugs attending two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (recruited June 2021 to March 2022), recent use of fentanyl test strips was less common a year after the start than at the start, and not clearly different after six months: the adjusted odds of having used strips in the past 30 days were 0.642 times those at the start at 12 months (95% CI 0.447 to 0.923; all 541 people) and 0.557 times (0.364 to 0.853) in the 212 who answered all three surveys, and 0.936 times (0.696 to 1.258) at 6 months, while the share of those 212 who had ever used strips rose from 65 to 80 in 100. The share using strips at each survey is not given in the main text (the supplement, which may give it, was not read), so the size of the fall cannot be given as a number out of 100. The 213 of the 541 who gave no follow-up had less often used strips than the 212 who answered all three surveys (54 against 65 in 100), which could bias the trend, and why use fell was not measured (the authors suggest that a test for fentanyl alone tells people less once fentanyl is expected). Over a few weeks, young adults in a Rhode Island pilot used a median of 3 of the 10 strips they were given (10 of 81 used all ten); in that pilot and in a British Columbia take-home programme, 95 or 96 in 100 said they would use strips again; the 49 to 96 in 100 that a scoping review relays across studies comes, by its supplementary table, from five figures in four studies, two of them these same programmes (95 in 100 each in its table) and the others 49 and 74 in 100 at two US syringe services programmes and 96 in 100 in a take-home study in Sydney, Australia; these are intentions rather than measures of use. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the one study that followed people for a year (people who inject drugs at two rural US programmes), fewer had used test strips recently after 12 months than at the start, though more had used them at some point. The study lost many people along the way and did not measure why use fell. In shorter studies about 95 in 100 said they would use strips again, but that is a plan, not a measure.

Lifetime use among complete cases 65.1% at baseline, 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months. No follow-up: 213 of 541 (39.4%, editors' calculation), who had less often used strips (54.3% against 65.1%). Krieger: median 3 strips (IQR 1–6) within a few weeks; 10 of 81 used all ten; 77/81 (95%) would like to use strips in future. Klaire: 322/336 answers (95.8%) would use strips again. Kutscher (relayed; Supplemental Table 2): would use strips again 49% (Baltimore, 123 participants) and 74% (Delaware, 102; Park et al., 2021), 96% if free (Sydney, 78; Sutherland et al., 2021), 95% (Rhode Island, 93; Krieger) and 95% (Vancouver, 218; Klaire); three other rows give ratings or descriptions.

statement: At one 25,000-capacity festival in England, the first year with an on-site drug checking service (2016, when chemists analysed 247 samples and staff gave results in 230 consultations, with alerts to on-site agencies), compared with the year before (2015): the evidence is insufficient to say whether the service changed drug-related hospital admissions. The festival's figures, from unpublished police reports, were 19 drug-related admissions among 59 admissions in 2015 and 1 among 50 in 2016; admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49 (editors' calculation), paramedics were said to have treated more people on site rather than sending them to hospital, the partner agencies' data used to judge such outcomes changed between years in the agencies employed and the indicators used and did not always separate drug-related from other incidents, and the author states that the pilot cannot show what part the service played. This was testing by chemists at one festival, with one year before and one after and no comparison festival; it says nothing about kits used at home. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: At one English festival, drug-related hospital admissions fell from 19 in 2015 to 1 in 2016, the first year chemists tested drugs on site. But other admissions rose, paramedics were said to have treated more people on site that year, and the data the agencies kept changed between years, so the study cannot show that the testing caused the fall. The author says the same.

exposure: The festival's first on-site drug checking service (2016): chemists' analysis (FTIR, colour reagents, mass loss) with a brief consultation, alerts to on-site agencies and festival-goers, and a disposal service
comparator: The same festival in 2015, without the service
outcome: Drug-related hospital admissions counted by the festival (from unpublished police post-event reports)
magnitude: Drug-related admissions 19 of 59 in 2015 against 1 of 50 in 2016 (a 95% fall as printed); admissions not classed as drug-related 40 then 49 (editors' calculation). No interval or test. No drug-related deaths at the festival in 2016, a year with six at UK festivals; the author notes that deaths at festivals are rare and often have several causes.

statement: In people who use drugs in the United States, mostly recruited at harm-reduction services, and in Canadian and European drug checking studies relayed by two reviews, people who use test strips or drug checking differ from people in the same samples who do not, though not in the same ways in every study: in the largest study they more often used fentanyl and injected and already did more to lower their risk, and in a rural cohort they more often used heroin and had seen an overdose, so simple comparisons of the two groups mix any effect of testing with who chooses to test. At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 people who had used strips in the past 30 days and 318 who had not differed in fentanyl use (78 against 59 in 100), injecting (75 against 57 in 100) and ever having been shown how to use strips (76 against 41 in 100); the strip group already reported more of the eight risk-reduction behaviours studied at the start (a median of 6 against 5; for example, 64 against 39 in 100 said naloxone was always nearby when they used), and its overdose rate was twice as high without adjustment and not clearly different with it (risk ratio 2.06, then 1.20). In rural people who inject drugs (recruited from 2021 and followed for a year), strip use went with having seen an overdose in the past 6 months (adjusted odds ratio 2.444, 95% CI 1.784 to 3.347), heroin use (1.615, 1.107 to 2.357) and being married or living as married (1.521, 1.084 to 2.134), and less with being unhoused (0.679, 0.504 to 0.913), but not clearly with having overdosed oneself (0.981, 0.676 to 1.424) or with fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948 to 1.872). In a small Rhode Island pilot, the 62 who used a strip differed clearly from the 19 who did not only in more often having sold drugs (84 against 58 in 100), and if anything had less often injected (47 against 68 in 100), while among those who used a strip, those whose strip showed fentanyl used heroin weekly far more often (20 of 31 against 3 of 31). A scoping review relays one Vancouver study in which drug checking services were used more by people who had seen an overdose in the past 6 months, suspected exposure to fentanyl, injected in public, did sex work or had had a non-fatal overdose (Beaulieu et al., 2020, as cited by Kutscher et al., 2024). In three European studies relayed by another review, clients of drug checking services used ecstasy more often than people in party settings who did not use the services, although in the largest of them people who used the services more often reported using ecstasy less often and less unsafe party behaviour. All characteristics were self-reported, and the two larger studies recruited people at harm-reduction services. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who use test strips are not the same as people who don't. In the largest US study they more often used fentanyl and injected, and already said they did more to lower their risk before it began: 64 in 100 said naloxone was always nearby when they used drugs, against 39 in 100 of those who did not use strips. In another study, more of them had seen an overdose. So comparing the two groups cannot tell us what the strips themselves do.
population: People who use drugs in the United States: 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); 541 people who inject drugs at two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (2021–2023); 81 young adults recruited by advertisement for a Rhode Island pilot (2017); European drug checking studies relayed by a systematic review; and one Vancouver study of drug checking services relayed by a scoping review

comparator: People in the same samples who did not use strips or services
outcome: Drug use, injecting, witnessing an overdose, housing, marital status and earlier risk-reduction behaviour, and how an overdose comparison changed after adjustment

statement: In people who use drugs given test strips or colour test kits to check their own drugs, handing out kits compared with not handing them out: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it causes harm, for example through false reassurance after a negative result, or reduces harm, and the question is disputed. No study read compared people given kits with people not given them on harm or overdose. What was measured shows few riskier responses: in a British Columbia take-home programme, 6 of 336 survey answers (2 in 100) described using alone or using more or faster after a strip showed fentanyl, in answer to standard questions, and the one study comparing overdoses in people who did and did not use strips found no clear difference after adjustment, in an imprecise estimate (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06). In the Rhode Island pilot, people were told that a negative strip does not rule out fentanyl and to take the same precautions whatever the result. But no primary study read reports what people did after a negative result: the take-home programme asked and did not report the answers, and at the supervised injection site staff recorded only intentions (to use less after 7 of 122 negative checks before use); a scoping review relays one programme in which 10 in 100 women reported a safer change after a negative strip, against 67 in 100 after a positive one. The same review relays people believing that a negative strip means xylazine or that the strength of the line shows how strong the fentanyl is, one person saying a negative result would mean using a little more, a positive result possibly leading people who do not use opioids to think they tolerate fentanyl, and strips giving no information on xylazine and some other drugs and, it says, missing carfentanil, which the laboratory studies read for this page detected on most brands and lots, though only at higher concentrations (see the answer on fentanyl analogues). With take-home strips, people reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples (28 in 100) and 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17 in 100), against 5 of 97 (5 in 100) and 1 of 92 (1 in 100) tested by staff on site, which the authors think more likely reflects how the tests were done than a different supply. Two critiques argue, without data, that frequent positive results without ill effects could breed complacency, that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result, and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe; one of them still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: No study has measured whether handing out test kits causes harm. When people were asked, few said they took more risks after a strip showed fentanyl (about 2 in 100 answers), and one study found no clear difference in overdoses. But the studies read said little about what people did after a strip showed no fentanyl, some people misread strips, strips do not show other drugs such as xylazine, and take-home strips showed fentanyl in stimulants far more often than staff found. Critics worry that a negative result may make people feel safe when they are not; this has not been measured.
population: People who use drugs given fentanyl test strips (North America, 2017–2023) or colour test kits for ecstasy (Europe, as discussed in 2001), and published critiques of self-testing
exposure: Handing out test kits for people to test their own drugs
comparator: Not handing out kits (no study read made this comparison directly)
outcome: Harms: riskier use after a result, false reassurance after a negative or reassuring result, complacency, misreading results; and overdose
magnitude: Klaire: riskier responses 6/336 answers (1.8%; Wilson 0.8–3.8%, editors' calculation), 1 using more or faster and 5 using alone; responses to a negative result asked but not reported; take-home strips against on-site checks, crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 points (14.8–30.1), cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), 16.1 (7.1–25.1). Vickers-Smith: nonfatal overdose adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89); composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (0.34–1.38) on 0–15, from models without the baseline score, which was already higher (median 8 against 7; eTable 4). Karamouzian: intended dose reduction after 7/122 negative checks before use (5.7%). Kutscher (relayed): riskier use in two studies (its refs 47 and 66, the second Klaire et al., whose 6 of 336 answers it gives as six participants, 1.8%); difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34%; Baltimore programme (103 women; Park et al., 2020, its ref. 80), safer change reported by 67% with a positive and 10% with a negative strip. No primary study read reports behaviour after a negative result.

grade.reasoning: Observational and narrative evidence, starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level: very low. Status contested: credible critiques (McGowan et al., 2018; Winstock et al., 2001) change how the early evidence is read, and the measured data lean towards benefit in what people say but show no measured benefit or harm on overdose. The claim does not rest only on narrative reviews: its measured data come from primary studies (Klaire et al., Vickers-Smith et al., Krieger et al., Karamouzian et al., Measham). Studies inside the two reviews are counted once: by the scoping review's Appendix 1, its six participants (1.8%) with riskier behaviour (ref. 66) are Klaire et al.'s 6 of 336 answers, and Klaire et al.'s 26 in 100 answers with a safer change are one of the eight values behind its median of 55 in 100.
