debate.question: Does handing out test strips to people who use drugs reduce harm, or can it cause harm, for example through false reassurance?
debate.evidence_yes: People who found fentanyl often said they then did things thought to lower overdose risk: of 31 young adults in Rhode Island with a positive strip, 45 in 100 said they used smaller amounts, 42 went slower and 39 used with someone else around (Krieger et al., 2018; sc_krieger_2018); at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to use less after 36 in 100 checks before use that showed fentanyl, against 6 in 100 that did not (Karamouzian et al., 2018; sc_karamouzian_2018); a scoping review relays a median of 55 in 100 reporting some safer change across seven studies, though by its supplementary table the top value counts changes after each positive result rather than people and another is the take-home programme's 26 in 100 answers (Kutscher et al., 2024; sc_kutscher_2024). At a festival where chemists tested drugs, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not as sold handed over drugs for destruction, observed by the service (Measham, 2019; sc_measham_2019). Over four weeks, people who used strips reported more risk-reduction behaviours than people who did not (adjusted difference 0.86 on a 0 to 15 score; for example naloxone nearby, risk ratio 1.10, 1.04 to 1.18), though they already reported more of them at the start (median score 8 against 7 out of 15), which the models did not adjust for (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025; sc_vickers_smith_2025). Riskier responses were rare when asked (6 of 336 answers; Klaire et al., 2022; sc_klaire_2022), and a vending-machine evaluation relayed by the scoping review reports county overdose deaths falling by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%. In the largest of three European studies, people who used drug checking services more often reported using ecstasy less often and less unsafe party behaviour (Maghsoudi et al., 2022; sc_maghsoudi_2022), and a festival evaluation relays reviews that found no rise in drug use, starting use or drug deaths in European countries with drug checking services compared with countries without them (country-level comparisons of services, not of kits; Measham, 2019, citing Brunt, 2012, and others; sc_measham_2019). The critique most cautious about self-testing still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone (McGowan et al., 2018; sc_mcgowan_2018).
debate.evidence_no: No study read shows that handing out strips prevents overdose or death: the only comparison of people who used strips with people who did not found no clear difference in self-reported overdose (adjusted risk ratio 1.20, 0.70 to 2.06; unadjusted 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89) (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025), and the scoping review found only 2 of 91 articles reporting overdose outcomes, neither comparing people who tested with people who did not (Kutscher et al., 2024). Most answers in the take-home programme described no change after a positive result (217 of 336; Klaire et al., 2022), few people intended to throw a drug away after a positive strip at the supervised injection site (11 in 100; Karamouzian et al., 2018), and the review relays people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl. Strips show only whether fentanyl is there, not how much, and as relayed they say nothing about xylazine and other drugs and may miss carfentanil (which the laboratory studies read for this page detected on most brands and lots, though only at higher concentrations); some people misread them (believing a negative means xylazine, or that the strength of the line shows how strong the fentanyl is), a positive result may lead people who do not use opioids to think they tolerate fentanyl (relayed by Kutscher et al., 2024), and with take-home strips people reported fentanyl in stimulant samples about 5 and 16 times as often as staff found on site (editors' calculation, the ratio of the two shares, from Klaire et al., 2022; sc_klaire_2022). Critiques argue that a negative result may falsely reassure (a Health Canada warning about false negatives, cited by McGowan et al., 2018), that frequent positives without ill effects could breed complacency and that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result (McGowan et al., 2018; sc_mcgowan_2018), and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe (Winstock et al., 2001; sc_winstock_2001), which also cites a survey in which 40 in 100 people at clubs said they would take more if pills were thought to have improved. In three European studies, people who used drug checking used ecstasy more often than people in party settings who did not (Maghsoudi et al., 2022; sc_maghsoudi_2022), which may reflect who chooses to test, and a festival evaluation relays critics' concerns, without data, that testing may give an artificial sense of safety and weaken the deterrent effect of drugs' risks by making them seem safer (Measham, 2019; sc_measham_2019).
debate.neither_can_show: Whether handing out strips changes overdose or death: the sources read contain no randomized or well-controlled comparison, and people who use strips differ from those who do not (more fentanyl use and injecting, more earlier risk reduction), so comparisons between them mix testing with who tests. Whether false reassurance happens, and how often: no primary study read reports what people did after a negative result (the supervised injection site recorded only intentions, and a review relays one programme's self-reports), and the harms in the critiques are reasoned, not measured. What people actually took after any result: apart from the festival handovers, the figures are self-reports, intentions or answers to standard questions from people who chose to test. Settings: almost all data come from North American services where fentanyl was common, and the colour-test critique concerns ecstasy pills in Europe around 2000.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the sources read, handing out test strips has not been shown either to cause harm or to prevent overdose. What people say leans towards benefit: after a positive result a minority to a majority report using less or more carefully, or say they intend to (Karamouzian et al., 2018; Krieger et al., 2018; Kutscher et al., 2024), and riskier responses were rare when asked (Klaire et al., 2022); but these are self-reports from people who chose to test and who already did more to lower their risk (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025). The harms the critiques describe (McGowan et al., 2018; Winstock et al., 2001) are plausible and unmeasured; the largest gap is what people do after a negative result, which no primary study read reports, although one programme asked (Klaire et al., 2022). The strips' own limits (no amount, missed drugs, misreading, positive readings with take-home strips for stimulants; Klaire et al., 2022; Kutscher et al., 2024; McGowan et al., 2018) are facts about the tests, rated in the test-accuracy claims, not evidence of what people then do. The single comparison of overdose is too imprecise to rule out either a benefit or a harm (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized trial or stepped roll-out of strip distribution across sites or areas, with naloxone and the same advice in both arms, recording what people do after positive and after negative results (verified where possible, for example by photographs of strips or laboratory checks of a share of samples), with overdose and death taken from emergency, hospital and death records; and studies that test the same samples at home and in a laboratory, so that how often people meet a false negative in real use is known.

statement: In the 50 US states and the District of Columbia from 2018 to 2022, a state law making fentanyl test strips legal, as dated by the authors (16 jurisdictions, from June 2018 to August 2022), compared with the same states before their law and with states the authors counted as having no such law at the time, is associated with fewer deaths from drug overdose than the comparison predicted, in one state-level study (Bhai et al., 2025; no funding, no conflicts declared): about 7% fewer per 100,000 residents (6.7%, 95% CI 1.4% to 11.7%, without adjustment; 7.1%, 3.4% to 10.7%, adjusted for age, rurality and income; editors' calculation from the reported coefficients), which at the death rate in state-months with a law is roughly 2.6 to 2.8 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents a year (editors' rough calculation). With adjustment the figures were similar for White (8.0%) and Black residents (8.4%), though for Black residents the event studies show death rates above the comparison in every pre-law month they cover (editors' reading of the figures); the abstract's 13.5% for Black residents is the unadjusted estimate (11.9%) converted with its sign reversed. Unintentional overdose deaths, set against overdose deaths by suicide, homicide or undetermined intent, were 5% to 8% lower, with weak support without adjustment and no difference for Black residents with adjustment (−0.2%; 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%). This is a study of laws in whole state populations, not of people who used strips: it can show that death rates in these states ran below the comparison after their laws, but not that the laws or the strips caused it, nor whether people who tested their drugs were less likely to die. It did not measure whether strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug rather than opioid or fentanyl deaths, and it did not allow for other state policies or for changes in each state's drug supply at the same time; the fall appears from the first month of a law, which is hard to explain by strips that first had to be handed out and used (editors' reading; the authors' own appendix argues that some laws made no real difference until months or years after taking effect), and the models used 2,613 of a possible 3,060 state-months without saying which were left out (editors' calculation). The law dates are the authors' own coding, set out in an online appendix added by a 2026 correction: each law's effective date from a legal database, except that they counted Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico, whose laws took effect in 2021 or 2022, as having no law through 2022, and dated North Carolina's 2019 law from July 2022 and the District of Columbia's April 2019 law from August 2019, on their reading of the laws and on pharmacist surveys and other reports, some from 2023 and 2025, after the study period; no results with the database's own dates are reported, and the appendix does not mention the six states that the paper's map shows as legal without a date. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one study of US states from 2018 to 2022, after a state made fentanyl test strips legal, drug deaths ran below what the trends in other states predicted: roughly 3 fewer deaths a year for every 100,000 people, or about 7 fewer for every 100 drug deaths expected. Results were about the same for White and Black residents once age, rural living and income were allowed for, though the result for Black residents is less certain. The study looked at laws and death records, not at people using strips. It did not check whether more strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug, and other changes at the same time could explain the difference. The researchers chose the law dates themselves: they counted Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico as having no law, though laws started there in 2021 and 2022, gave two other laws later dates than their source did, and showed no results using the source's dates.
population: All residents of the 50 US states and the District of Columbia, 2018 to 2022, counted through state-by-month death and population records; White and Black residents also analysed separately
exposure: A state law making fentanyl test strips legal, in force and judged by the authors to be a meaningful policy change (16 jurisdictions, June 2018 to August 2022, dated by the authors: each law's effective date from a legal database, except that Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico, whose laws took effect in 2021 or 2022, were counted as having no law, and North Carolina and the District of Columbia were dated later than the database; Online Appendix A)
comparator: The same states before their law and states the authors counted as having no such law at the time, which include Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico throughout and North Carolina before July 2022, although the legal database dates a strip law in each within the period (imputation difference-in-differences with state and month fixed effects); for unintentional deaths, also overdose deaths by suicide, homicide or undetermined intent in the same states and months
outcome: Deaths from overdose of any drug (labelled drug-induced deaths in the paper's tables) per 100,000 residents per month, and unintentional drug-overdose deaths; opioid- and fentanyl-specific deaths were not analysed
magnitude: Bhai et al. 2025, Table 3 (log death rate; coefficient and SE clustered by state): whole population −0.069 (0.028) without and −0.074 (0.020) with controls; all races −0.075 (0.030) and −0.078 (0.021); White −0.077 (0.032) and −0.083 (0.023); Black −0.127 (0.028) and −0.088 (0.026). As percentages (the paper's 100(e^β − 1); 95% CI editors' calculation): whole population −6.7% (−11.7% to −1.4%) and −7.1% (−10.7% to −3.4%); White −7.4% and −8.0%; Black −11.9% (the abstract's 13.5% is this value with the sign reversed) and −8.4%. Absolute (editors' rough calculation): about 0.22 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents per month against a mean of 3.03 in state-months with a law, roughly 2.6 to 2.8 per 100,000 a year. Table 4, unintentional against other-intent overdose deaths: whole population −0.053 (0.032) and −0.056 (0.027) (−5.2%, −5.4%); White −0.070 (0.037) and −0.082 (0.031); Black −0.058 (0.029) and −0.002 (0.026; −0.2%, 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%).

evidence.extracted: The authors list as limitations state-level data that may hide local variation, possible inconsistencies across states in how overdose deaths are classified or reported, and a study period of only 5 years; they did not measure community groups providing strips, did not consider strip use in states where strips are prohibited, and note that other state policies, including those relevant to hospital administration, may affect overdose deaths.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious on the card (sc_bhai_2025): no adjustment for other state policies, federal strip funding from 2021 or changes in each state's drug supply; laws were adopted where death rates were higher; the event-study pre-period intervals are wide, and for Black residents every pre-period point lies above zero, with several 95% bands wholly above it (editors' reading of Figures 3 and 4); the fall appears from the month of the law; the exposure is the authors' own coding, which departs from the legal database for five jurisdictions (three states' 2021–2022 laws counted as absent, two dated later), partly on evidence from after the study period, with no results shown for the database's dates, and six jurisdictions shaded legal on the map have no date and are not mentioned in the authors' appendix; outcome codes are not given; 2,613 of a possible 3,060 state-months are used without explanation (1,469 for Black residents).

inconsistency.note: Single study. Within it, the unintentional-death estimate for Black residents with controls is null (−0.2%), which is stated rather than rated.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: laws and deaths from any drug overdose in US state populations, 2018 to 2022. As evidence on whether using strips prevents deaths it would be indirect (no measure of strip access or use), and it is not cited for that.

imprecision.note: The interval for the main estimate runs from about 1% to 12% fewer deaths without adjustment and 3% to 11% with it (editors' calculation), from a trivial to a sizeable difference; 16 jurisdictions changed law, four of them with at most 7 months of data after it, and clustered standard errors with few treated states can understate uncertainty.

plausible_confounding.note: Remaining confounding could run either way (laws adopted as deaths peaked would favour an apparent fall); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down for risk of bias and for imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Worded as an association: a state-level comparison of laws cannot show that the laws, or the strips, caused the lower death rates, and it says nothing about what happened to the people who tested their drugs. Single study: no other study of these laws and deaths was cited by the paper or read.
